qa_notes: Clean extraction of a full IJCAI-18 paper; QA4 scored 0 because SOLA is semi-supervised online AUC/ML (stochastic gradient/saddle-point is SGD, not a named PM or stochastic-process technique); QA8 scored 1 because AUC is a closely analogous ranking/accuracy metric; QA7 scored 0 because the Madeyski & Kawalerowicz (2017) CI dataset is cited but no code or data URL is provided. FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (CI build-outcome prediction, not process mining or stochastic process modeling).
research_question: How can a semi-supervised online AUC optimization method (SOLA) jointly handle streaming CI events, scarce build-outcome labels, class imbalance, and suspiciousness ranking so that likely-successful builds can be skipped and CI build effort reduced?
main_finding: On eight GitHub/CI projects from the Madeyski & Kawalerowicz continuous-defect-prediction dataset, SOLA attains mean AUC 0.783, beating Hoeffding Tree (0.551), OMR (0.539) and online AUC-only SOLAM (0.741), matching the batch upper bound SAMULT (0.782) while cutting model-update time by more than 97% versus batch learning, indicating that addressing the four CI prediction challenges together reduces wasted successful-build effort.
limitations: Evaluation uses only eight open-source Java projects; authors note that results may not generalize to closed-source or non-Java systems and plan broader experiments and richer (e.g. deep) features.

qa_notes: Clean book-chapter extraction (arXiv v2); survey/tutorial with Jupyter demonstrations on public Jira data rather than a single empirical study. QA4/QA8 scored 0: techniques are NLP/embeddings/link analysis, not a named process-mining or stochastic-modeling method, and the chapter's own demos report cosine similarity and sentiment rather than fitness/precision/F1. QA6 scored 0: 'Pitfalls and Takeaways' discuss NLP false positives, not study threats to validity. QA7 scored 1 (Zenodo notebooks + Jira dataset DOI + LYNX GitHub). FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (MSR/NLP on issue trackers, not PM/stochastic SE modeling).
research_question: How can NLP and mining techniques applied to issue-tracker content, metadata, discussions, evolution histories, and issue links help stakeholders analyse requirements quality, issue evolution, comments, and traceability in large heterogeneous issue repositories?
main_finding: Four demonstrated use cases on public Jira data (including the Montgomery et al. 2.7M-issue dataset) show that lexical/POS/hypernym methods can flag subjective language and nominalisations in user stories, description edits often reduce sentiment toward more technical wording, comment mining can surface suggested field updates, and TF-IDF vs BERT embeddings distinguish Cloner links (highest similarity) while Duplicate links are not reliably separable from other types by text similarity alone.
limitations: Issue text is heterogeneous and often low-quality (false-positive ambiguity detections; 'Story' issues that are not true user stories; sentiment tools sensitive to URLs/log dumps); typed issue-link classification remains an open problem (cited macro-F1 still modest); the chapter is a methods survey with illustrative analyses rather than a controlled experiment.

qa_notes: Clean ICSE'14 extraction; Monte-Carlo simulation is formally named (QA4=1) and applied to the published SAS/GuideArch architecture case. QA8 scored 0: reported quantities are expected net benefit, loss probability, project-failure risk and EVTPI/EVPPI, not process-model quality or predictive accuracy metrics. QA6 scored 1 via the Evaluation section (model falsifiability, elicitation bias, scalability, applicability) even without a 'Threats to Validity' heading. Tool/models claimed at cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/e.letier/sdda (QA7=1).
research_question: How can statistical decision analysis — eliciting parameter uncertainty as probability distributions, propagating it with Monte-Carlo simulation, shortlisting architectures on expected net benefit versus risk, and computing expected value of information — support early software requirements and architecture decisions?
main_finding: Reanalysing the SAS emergency-response architecture model (6,912 candidates, 175 uncertain parameters), Monte-Carlo simulation plus a resolution-margin Pareto strip shortlists nine architectures with higher expected net benefit and much lower project-failure risk than GuideArch's top ten; EVTPI is only 0.25% of best ENB, so further reducing parameter uncertainty has little decision value given the current (non-falsifiable) utility model.
limitations: Authors themselves stress that the SAS utility/contribution model is not falsifiable, so rankings and information-value estimates cannot be empirically validated; the method does not yet treat model (structural) uncertainty; expert probability-elicitation methods have not been evaluated in software engineering; political/governance barriers to honest uncertainty reporting remain untested.

qa_notes: Clean TOSEM 1997 survey/assessment of PSEE technology (OIKOS, EPOS, SPADE-1). QA4 scored 1 because SLANG/SPADE Petri nets (ER nets) and related PMLs are formally named; this is process modeling/enactment, not process mining (pm_technique=other). QA3/QA5/QA7/QA8 scored 0: no reproducible event log or dataset, no new empirical validation (industrial notes cite prior work; authors admit industrial experience is still limited), no artefacts, no fitness/precision-style metrics (Sutton 'fitness' here means human followability). FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (1990s PSEE survey, not PM or stochastic modeling of SE processes).
research_question: How can process-centered software engineering environments (PSEEs) and their process-modeling languages be systematically compared, and what is the state of the art when OIKOS, EPOS, SPADE-1 and related systems are assessed on a shared grid covering PML technology, architecture, and industrial experience?
main_finding: A three-part assessment grid applied to OIKOS, EPOS, SPADE-1 and related PSEEs shows that Petri-net and rule-based PMLs can support process analysis, simulation and enactment, but industrial uptake is constrained by low process-maturity (CMM 1–2 organisations need comprehension/simulation more than enactment), lack of incremental introduction strategies, and the trade-off between advanced research platforms and commercially interoperable technology.
limitations: Authors state that industrial use of the three research prototypes remains limited and ISPW reference examples are insufficient for real evaluation; the grid needs refinement for early lifecycle phases, user interfaces and metaprocesses; no shared reference PSEE architecture exists, making comparative assessment inherently biased.

qa_notes: Clean arXiv extraction of a large mixed-methods MSR paper; explicit RQs, Zenodo dataset/code (QA7=1), and a full Wohlin-style threats section (QA6=1). QA4 scored 0: no named process-mining or stochastic-modeling technique (descriptive mining of YAML workflow diffs). QA8 scored 0: results are frequencies/medians/%, not fitness/precision/F1/MAPE-style quality metrics. FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (CI/CD configuration evolution, not PM/stochastic SE modeling).
research_question: How frequently and in which conceptual/syntactic ways do GitHub Actions workflow files change over time, and is there evidence that LLM coding tools or other major technological shifts have changed workflow creation or maintenance frequency?
main_finding: On 236,775 workflow histories from 47,488 popular GitHub repositories (Nov 2019–Aug 2025), repositories have a median of three workflow files and about 7.3% of files change each week; ~79% of changesets are modification-only and ~80% of edits concentrate in job steps (task specification/configuration); Dependabot (69%) and Renovate (21%) drive many Action version updates toward more secure pinning; before/after tests found no conclusive effect of LLM tools on change frequency.
limitations: Dataset is restricted to active, popular GitHub repos (≥300 stars and commits); 11.54% of histories with invalid YAML were dropped; only the primary branch is observed (squash merges can hide fine-grained changes); LLM-impact analysis is a coarse before/after design that cannot reliably detect agent use.

qa_notes: Clean ESEC/FSE'19 extraction; six Gerrit communities with Table 1 counts, GitHub replication package, and an explicit Threats to Validity section. QA4 scored 0: review-linkage-graph recovery plus TF-IDF classifiers is MSR/traceability, not a named process-mining or stochastic-modeling technique. QA8 scored 1 for reported precision/recall/F1/AUC of link-category classifiers and reviewer recommenders. FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (code-review analytics / artefact linkage, not PM or stochastic process models).
research_question: To what degree are modern code reviews linked, why are they linked, can link categories be recovered automatically from surrounding text, and does using linked-review information available at prediction time improve reviewer recommendation and review-outcome prediction?
main_finding: Among 1.47M Gerrit reviews, linkage rates range from 3% to 25% (25% OpenStack, 17% Chromium) and 16 link types fall into five categories; classifiers recover categories with F1 0.71–0.79 (more than double ZeroR); adding linkage awareness improves cHRev reviewer-recommender F1 by 37–88% (5–14 percentage points), while outcome predictors misclassify 35–39% of linked reviews.
limitations: Regex recovery may miss or falsely extract links (manual false-positive rate <0.1% in the coded sample); open coding is subjective despite dual-coder agreement; classifiers and impact analyses focus on OpenStack Nova/Neutron and may not generalise to all Gerrit or non-Gerrit review environments.

qa_notes: IEEE APSEC 2012 CSP/PAT conformance-checking paper; running example is bank account-opening and the 50 InFlux models are from general business domains, so QA2 scored 0 (not an SE-specific process context). QA4/QA8 scored 1 (named conformance checking via CSP trace refinement; fitness, closeness, structural/behavioural appropriateness in Table IV). QA6/QA7 scored 0: no threats-to-validity discussion and no public logs/code (in-house InFlux + PAT). FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (generic BPM conformance, not software-engineering processes).
research_question: How can Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) and automated trace-refinement checking in PAT verify whether MXML event logs conform to arbitrary/unstructured BPMN-style reference processes, and what fitness, closeness and appropriateness metrics can be derived from the resulting counterexamples?
main_finding: Translating BPMN processes and logs into trace-equivalent CSP processes reduces conformance to PAT trace-refinement, identifying all non-replayable traces; on 50 InFlux industrial models checking is fast (mean analysis time 0.034–0.044s); on the bank-account running example, logs 1–2 have fitness/closeness 1.0 while noisy log 3 has fitness 0.886 and closeness 0.389, with structural appropriateness 0.607.
limitations: Exceptions are not handled; checking whether the model conforms to the log fails on infinite traces; the 50-model experiment uses CPN-generated logs (with injected noise) rather than independently observed field logs; CSP encodings can be complex, though they are hidden from the end user.

qa_notes: IEEE two-column extract is complete and readable (minor hyphenation); QA3/QA5 scored 0 because Section V is only a constructed Incremental-Development illustration with assumed triangular PDFs, not a real project log; no threats-to-validity discussion, no shared data/code, and the KS bound is a Monte Carlo sample-size rule rather than a process-model quality metric.
research_question: How can a UML Activity-Diagram well-formed process model, combined with Monte Carlo sampling of resource-constrained deterministic activity networks, yield the probability distribution of software-development-process duration when resources are constrained and activities may loop?
main_finding: A restricted UML Activity-Diagram WFP plus Monte Carlo GenerateDAN/ScheduleDAN (heuristic RCPSP scheduling) produces an empirical PDF/CDF of SDP duration; on an illustrative four-package Incremental Development example, 4,649 scenarios give 1,810 ± 36.2 hours (227 ± 5 calendar days) at 95% confidence and 2% KS error.
limitations: Assumes the SDP can be expressed as a well-formed process and that business allocation policy maps to a single priority heuristic; uses a restricted UML subset; demonstrated only on a constructed example with assumed activity PDFs, with no comparison of predicted versus observed durations.

qa_notes: Clean, complete BPMDS/LNCS position paper; QA3/QA5 scored 0 because the only concrete log is a toy VCS excerpt and the 'two-year real-world pull-request dataset' is unnamed, while reported results are citations to prior papers [4,6,7] and usefulness is left to future user studies; no threats-to-validity, data/code, or fitness-style metrics.
research_question: What can be discovered from software-development data (VCS, ITS, and unstructured comments) to obtain process knowledge across the time, case, organizational, and control-flow perspectives?
main_finding: This research-in-progress position paper argues that process mining can be extended to software repositories by mining Gantt-style time views, artifact-evolution cases, NLP-inferred resource roles, and pull-request control-flow; proof-of-concept pointers are given to prior papers, but no new empirical validation is reported here.
limitations: Authors flag time-approximation/granularity/coverage issues for VCS timestamps, NLP brittleness on developer jargon, and hard case/activity identification; control-flow discovery and usefulness evaluation via user studies are explicitly left as future work.

qa_notes: Full text is clean and complete; NetBeans public artifacts and dated URLs (Issuezilla, XTest, QA graphs) are specified well enough for QA3=1, and the authors did discover/model/re-enact a real process (QA5=1); QA6/QA7/QA8 scored 0 because challenges are discussed without a threats-to-validity framing, no research dataset/code is released, and conformance is only informal role/artifact/tool reconciliation (no fitness/precision).
research_question: Can software processes of large global OSSD projects (illustrated on the NetBeans requirements-and-release process) be discovered, modeled, and re-enacted from publicly observable Web information spaces using a process meta-model and reference model?
main_finding: A bottom-up Web-artifact discovery strategy guided by the Mi–Scacchi meta-model produced informal (use cases, rich hypermedia, flow graphs) and formal PML models of the NetBeans requirements-and-release process that could be compiled into navigable re-enactments; walkthroughs surfaced practical issues such as release-manager overload and duplicated testing work across four agent types.
limitations: Private communications are unobservable; ethnographic discovery does not scale across many projects; assembling control-flow and activity hierarchy from heterogeneous artifacts remains largely manual; process prescriptions may not match actual enactment; demonstration is concentrated on one NetBeans process (Mozilla/Apache mentioned only as further cases).

qa_notes: Short, clean OSS 2007 paper; QA3 scored 0 because the seven case studies name Apache/Mozilla/NetBeans public portals but give no artifact inventory, time window (beyond 'circa 2002' for the seed surveys), or coding protocol that would allow reproduction; qualitative application experiences support QA5=1, but there is no threats section, shared data/code, or model-quality metric.
research_question: Does a reference-model mapping from OSS project-artifact terms to a taxonomy of agents, resources, tools, and actions provide a systematic way to code evidence and discover OSS processes across projects and process types?
main_finding: A Mi–Scacchi-based reference-model dictionary guided discovery in seven case studies (NetBeans, Apache HTTPD, Mozilla): it was adequate for development/release/testing processes, too coarse for interorganizational process communication (missing proper names of shared libraries/tools and cross-project vocabularies), and useful for detecting role-migration tracks from shifts in an individual's action-taxonomy branches.
limitations: The reference model cannot eliminate discovery risk from cross-project lexical variance; usage-pattern data were especially limited; much interorganizational evidence lies outside public portals; full automated coding is judged not yet attainable; the model addresses only the data-analysis stage of process discovery.

qa_notes: Complete ICPM 2022 paper; two-column wrap artifacts but fully assessable; QA2 scored 0 because the contribution and all evaluation logs (pharmacy, insurance, loan, P2P, confidential CF, BPIC 2012/2017) are generic business-process simulation, not software engineering; QA8 credited for precision/recall, SMAPE, and Wasserstein/EMD between simulated and real temporal distributions.
research_question: Given an event log and a BPS model, can extraneous (non-resource-contention) activity delays be discovered and injected as timer events so that the enhanced model replicates the log's temporal dynamics more accurately than the original BPS model?
main_finding: Estimating each activity instance's optimal start (max of enablement time via a Heuristics Miner concurrency oracle and resource-availability time) and fitting timer-event delay distributions—optionally TPE-scaled—re-discovers injected extraneous delays (precision 1.00; recall 1.00 except 0.75 on P2P-4) and reduces cycle-time/timestamp EMD versus SIMOD baselines on BPIC 2012 and 2017.
limitations: Resource-contention waiting can partially or totally eclipse extraneous delays (missed P2P timer); first-activity delays are discarded because trace arrival is not estimated; delays are attached only to the succeeding activity; evaluation uses five simulated plus two real-life processes and as-is replay rather than what-if prediction; construct validity depends on the chosen discretized-distribution distances.

qa_notes: Full QoSA 2016 text is clean and complete; QA6 scored 0 because there is no threats-to-validity discussion (fault-injection representativeness, workload, sequential-composition assumption are not treated as validity threats); QA8 scored 0 because validation uses reliability/%-diff tables, not fitness/precision/F1/MAPE/RMSE-style process-model quality metrics; raw data URL is given (QA7=1).
research_question: Can a discrete-time Markov chain that explicitly models error masking, propagation, recovery, and Avizienis multiple failure modes predict software-component reliability more accurately than classical two-state models, as validated by fault injection on Xen?
main_finding: An eight-state DTMC (OK/Error/Fail plus content/timing/hang/erratic and Halt) parameterized from Xen fault-injection runs (HVM n=1028, PV n=968, Dom0 Qemu/Watchdog) matches measured reliability within about 0–3.9% (mean absolute difference 0.69%), substantially closer than a classical no-recovery model (e.g. 85.22% vs real 97.86% on HVM); PV is more reliable than HVM, and Dom0 faults propagate to guest VMs while guest-to-guest isolation holds.
limitations: Only sequential component interaction is modeled (parallel/concurrent styles left as future work); faults are synthetic transient register bit-flips, not field failures; no dedicated threats-to-validity analysis; automated generation of the DTMC from an architecture is only planned.

qa_notes: IEEE two-column extract is complete enough to judge (some math OCR such as s, for s′); QA2 scored 0 because both real logs are e-government property registration and hospital ambulatory care, not software engineering; QA7=0 because only a Java/GraphViz prototype is 'available on request' and the logs are not released; support/confidence and a visual Alpha comparison are not fitness/precision/MAPE-style model-quality metrics (QA8=0); no threats-to-validity section.
research_question: How can sequential pattern mining (GSP) plus redundancy filtering and outlier search reconstruct workflows that domain experts find meaningful, and expose both frequent patterns and affiliated rare tasks, from transaction logs?
main_finding: GSP-based sequence mining with length-based filtering, a confidence-range (RoC) control, and a second GSP pass for outliers produced expert-interpretable workflows on a one-year Chinese e-government log (656,952 entries / 150,853 instances / 568 tasks) and a hospital log (52,237 entries / 11,702 instances / 18 tasks); domain experts preferred these graphs to the ProM Alpha model, which they found too tangled to understand.
limitations: Meaningfulness is judged qualitatively by domain-expert feedback rather than process-model quality metrics; results depend on user-chosen support/RoC thresholds; the e-government and hospital logs and the prototype are not publicly deposited (prototype only 'on request').

qa_notes: Readable IEEE extraction with some garbled math/operators but methods and tables remain assessable. QA6=0: no threats-to-validity discussion (conclusion is two sentences). QA7=0: ISBSG R9 is a licensed repository and authors only mention Zhu's unpublished R implementation of adaptive HLASSO, with no public data/code release.
research_question: How can software metric models with incomplete project samples be simplified (continuous-predictor omission and categorical-level collapse) by combining k-NN multiple imputation, Monte Carlo completion, and adaptive hierarchical LASSO, and does this outperform stepwise regression?
main_finding: On a preprocessed ISBSG R9 sample (669 of 3024 projects) predicting first-month extreme defects from major/minor defects, user-base locations, function points and development type, both stepwise and HLASSO drop the redundant locations predictor and merge enhancement with new-development; HLASSO keeps only the quadratic function-point term and reports lower K-fold CV MSE (71.51 vs 73.86) and MRE than stepwise.
limitations: Single ISBSG case; MRE is pathologically large because zero extreme-defect outcomes were replaced by 1e-6 in the denominator; no threats-to-validity section; licensed data and no released analysis code; theoretical properties of the imputation-plus-selection pipeline are not established.

qa_notes: Long SPE paper; extraction is clean aside from Wiley download watermarks. QA7=1: DeMaP Miner source is on GitHub (https://github.com/sharmapn/DeMaPMiner); data available from the corresponding author on request. QA8=1: framework accuracy 82% on 200 sentences with TP/TN/FP/FN, plus Cohen's kappa (0.67–0.78) and Fleiss 0.73 — treated as closely analogous to precision/F1. Process models are visualized (Disco) but fitness/precision of the mined nets are not reported.
research_question: What enacted Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) decision-making process can be mined from 1.54 million mailing-list emails, how does it differ from advertised/prior models, and how do Process, Informational and Standards Track PEP processes compare?
main_finding: DeMaP Miner (IR/NLP + process-mining visualization) on 463 PEPs / 89,914 decision-related emails (1995–2018) yields an enacted process with 48 new decision sub-states, 199 new pathways and 6 new stages (e.g. consensus formation, polling, voting) versus advertised PEP-1/prior state models; Standards Track PEPs are substantially more complex than Process/Informational PEPs; extraction accuracy 82% and a Python Steering Council member judged the mined model useful.
limitations: Single OSS community (Python) and mixed meritocracy/dictatorship era ending at BDFL resignation (2018); manual concept coding on 30 PEPs; NLP/ClausIE misses some triples and negation; off-list IRC/Twitter/F2F decisions unobserved; Disco maps are huge (61 activities, 235 paths) so figures show only a subset of paths; framework not yet applied to non-numbered-proposal projects (Apache, Linux, Perl).

qa_notes: Clean extraction. QA2=0: running example is a B2B purchase choreography (quote request/accept), not a software-engineering development process. QA4=1 because conformance checking / weak bisimulation / CCS are formally named, but this is model-checking equivalence of ebBP-ST vs WS-BPEL, not event-log process-mining conformance. QA5=0: only a 'towards' method plus 'preliminary' CWB checks on the toy use case and injected faults; no systematic empirical evaluation.
research_question: How can conformance between ebBP-ST choreographies and corresponding WS-BPEL control-process orchestrations be checked automatically by transforming both to CCS and testing weak bisimulation?
main_finding: Authors give algorithms that map well-formed binary ebBP-ST shared-state choreographies and WS-BPEL implementation patterns to CCS, then use the Edinburgh Concurrency Workbench to decide weak bisimulation; they argue the backend-driven B2Bi architecture requires this stricter notion rather than incoming/outgoing trace refinement. Only preliminary CWB applicability is claimed.
limitations: Restricted to well-formed binary ebBP-ST (no forks/joins, no overlapping shared states); BPEL must follow known ebBP implementation patterns rather than arbitrary processes; no public tool/data and no quantitative quality metrics; authors themselves list ongoing work on relaxing BPEL structure and usability (highlighting mismatches in the original models).

qa_notes: Used ft_0016_decoded.txt (+29 ASCII shift). Prose is readable; punctuation/quotes remain noisy and some math tokens are garbled. QA2=0: motivating domain is knowledge-intensive / unstructured processes (healthcare guidelines, ERP/CRM/BPMS), not a software-engineering process. QA5=0: this paper only describes the BIG4ProM plug-in and a toy deletion-trace IG; empirical evaluation is deferred to prior ESWA 2016 [11]. QA7=0: implemented as a ProM plug-in but no release URL or availability statement.
research_question: How can instance graphs be built from minimal event logs of unstructured, knowledge-intensive processes (filtering discovery plus repair of irregular traces), and how can that Building Instance Graph (BIG) algorithm be delivered as a ProM plug-in for both standard and expert users?
main_finding: BIG4ProM implements BIG in ProM: causal relations from α-algorithm, Heuristics Miner or infrequent Inductive Miner; irregular traces detected via PNetReplayer cost-based fitness alignments; deleted/inserted events are repaired so IGs stay connected and more precise; two variants (log-only with defaults vs expert-supplied Petri net + alignment); graphs are visualized and exported as DOT.
limitations: Current implementation requires Petri-net models and PNetReplayer-format alignments; no empirical study or quality-metric numbers in this paper; default miner parameters for non-expert users; not evaluated on software-engineering logs.

qa_notes: Short workshop-style paper; text is readable with minor formula/layout glitches. QA6=0: no threats-to-validity section (only a brief future-work caveat). QA7=0: Foundation GitHub is public but extracted issue time series and GSRM fitting code are not released. QA8=1: RSS and AIC are reported (RSS treated as closely analogous to RMSE).
research_question: Can a generalized software reliability model (GSRM) based on an Ito stochastic differential equation, applied after splitting OSS history by version, predict release dates and issue counts better than a classical NHPP reliability-growth model?
main_finding: On Zurb Foundation versions 2–4 (GitHub issues), GSRM obtains better AIC/RSS than NHPP and is claimed to predict release timing/issue volume better, but NHPP tracks the observed growth curve more closely and GSRM badly over-predicts (e.g. v2: 899 issues / 854 days vs actual 536 / 258). Time-independent growth rate was imposed so NHPP could be compared.
limitations: Single OSS project; growth-rate time-dependence was disabled for comparability, which the authors say prevented GSRM from fitting well; no threats-to-validity discussion; no released analysis code or extracted series; Table II predictions are far from actuals despite the 'successfully predict' claim in the conclusion.

qa_notes: ASE 2001 submission extract; some mojibake (smart quotes, math glyphs) but the argument is fully readable. QA3=1: CMM2 source (Paulk et al., pp. 125–191), encoding size (55 items, 27 actions, 79/150 edges), chance ranges 0.7X–1.3X, 2000/4000 runs and treatment-search settings are specified. QA7=0: 'full model available via email from the authors' is not a public archive. QA8=0: outcomes are class-worth ratios and treatment rankings, not fitness/precision/F1/MAPE/RMSE.
research_question: In data-starved early-lifecycle SE, can stochastic simulation of a subjective CMM level-2 knowledge model, summarized by the TAR2 treatment learner, identify a small set of management actions that improve the odds of cheap, high-chance projects (the 'minimal management question')?
main_finding: 2000 random JANE walks over an encoded CMM2 oracle, classified into cost×chance bands and summarized by TAR2, yield a handful of high-leverage treatments (notably lowering cost of using requirements, formal milestone reviews, and good unit testing) that raise 'worth' from 1.0 to about 1.28–1.44; most of the 27 candidate CMM2 actions can be ignored. Treatments remained stable when the sample was doubled to 4000 runs.
limitations: CMM2 is not universally accepted and the authors' subjective encoding may diverge from the SEI text; results come from simulated behaviour of that oracle, not field project data; random-search coverage is only checked by doubling N; a particular project may need fixed bindings that were not empirically validated. External-validity threats are discussed in §4.

qa_notes: IJSEKE 2023 extract is readable despite watermark/ligature noise. QA3=0: no empirical process log or simulation dataset — only Prolog encodings of assumed cause–effect relations. QA4=1: software-process simulation (PAS) is formally named; system dynamics appears in related work but is not the proposed technique. QA5=0: 'experiment' is SWI-Prolog queries showing the extended meta-model can mention quality; the PAS extension is not implemented or run on SE projects (authors say it still 'has to be changed').
research_question: How should the authors' Process Analysis Studio (PAS) simulation of software production be extended so that quality-related factors (QRFs) can influence, and be dynamically influenced by, simulated software-engineering-economics outcomes?
main_finding: Design-science proposal: wrap each PAS actor reaction with preQAction/postQAction hooks on an IPerforming interface so quality can affect KPIs before work and update itself afterwards (enabling feedback). Prolog queries on a simplified PAS 5.1.16 model succeed for possibleImpactAnalysis(quality, cost) and hasDynamicImpact only after those steps are asserted; no runtime simulation results are reported.
limitations: Evaluation is a subjective logical encoding of assumed CaERs, not an empirical or calibrated simulation study; the enhanced PAS is not implemented; no threats-to-validity section; no public code/data; authors note the proposal is PAS-specific and still needs performance and cross-tool evaluation after implementation.

qa_notes: FILE IS A FULL CEUR PROCEEDINGS DUMP (PNSE'15 + ADECS'15, CEUR-WS Vol. 1372, eds. Moldt/Rölke/Störrle), not a primary study. Title page, preface and table of contents confirm a workshop volume (2 invited talks, 7 full papers, 8 short papers, posters). Rated as a catalog item only — individual papers inside were not scored. QA1=1 solely because the preface states the workshop aim (Petri nets for modelling/validation/verification in SE). All empirical criteria 0.
research_question: Not a single-study research question; the volume's stated theme is how Petri nets (and extensions) can support modelling, validation and verification in software engineering, including adaptive discrete-event control (ADECS'15).
main_finding: This catalog PDF is the complete PNSE'15 workshop proceedings (Brussels, June 2015), not one research paper; it compiles invited talks, long/short presentations and posters on Petri nets in software engineering. No single empirical claim can be attributed to the volume as a whole.
limitations: Cannot be quality-assessed as a primary study: mixing heterogeneous papers would invalidate SLR QA/extraction; no unified dataset, method, validation, threats discussion, or process-model metrics apply at volume level.
